## Definition

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $N\ge1$, and for $0\le n\le N$ let $U_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_n}$ be open. A finite parameterized state-step graph consists of a $C^1$ initial map $x_0:\Theta\to U_0$ and $C^1$ step maps $\Psi_n:U_n\times\Theta\to U_{n+1}$ for $0\le n<N$, such that the recursion $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$ is defined for every $\theta$ in the chosen parameter neighborhood. A $C^1$ running objective consists of maps $\ell_n:U_n\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and a terminal objective $\phi:U_N\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, all $C^1$. Its reduced objective is
$$J(\theta)=\phi(x_N(\theta),\theta)+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\ell_n(x_n(\theta),\theta).$$
The maps and objective define one finite real-arithmetic graph. A gradient of this graph is the derivative of this finite composition; it is not the derivative of an exact implicit solution unless the step map itself is that solution map.

## Definition

Let $V$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and write $V^*$ for the continuous real dual. A parameter-dependent coercive elliptic variational problem is a family of bounded bilinear forms $a_\theta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ and bounded linear functionals $\ell_\theta\in V^*$ such that, on each parameter neighborhood under discussion, $\|a_\theta\|\le M$ and $a_\theta(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$ for fixed $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$. Operator-norm $C^1$ data means that the maps $\theta\mapsto A_\theta\in\mathcal L(V,V^*)$, $A_\theta u:=a_\theta(u,\cdot)$, and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta\in V^*$ are continuously Fréchet differentiable. A state at $\theta$ is a vector $u_\theta\in V$ satisfying $a_\theta(u_\theta,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ for every $v\in V$. When a state is specified, a $C^1$ objective $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ defines the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$. This definition alone asserts neither state existence nor uniqueness of an optimizer.

## Definition

Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple and let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open. A parameter-dependent parabolic variational problem specifies, for each $\theta\in\Theta$, a bilinear form $a_\theta(t;\cdot,\cdot)$ and data $f_\theta\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$, $u_{0,\theta}\in H$. A state is a function $u_\theta\in W(0,T;V)$ with continuous $H$ trace, $u_\theta(0)=u_{0,\theta}$, and
$$\langle u_\theta'(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}+a_\theta(t;u_\theta(t),v)=\langle f_\theta(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}$$
for every $v\in V$ and almost every $t$. When a state is specified, a differentiable terminal and running objective $\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T L(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt$ defines its reduced objective. This definition does not assert existence, parameter differentiability, or optimality.

## Statement

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\Theta$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuously differentiable. Let $V_\theta\subseteq\Theta$ be open and $u_0:V_\theta\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^1$. Assume there is a bounded convex open set $O\subset D$ with compact closure in $D$ such that for every $\theta\in V_\theta$ the unique solution of $u'=f(t,u,\theta)$, $u(0)=u_0(\theta)$, exists on $[0,T]$, and all triples $(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)$ lie in $O$. Then $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is $C^1$ as a map to $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$. For any $\theta_0\in V_\theta$, its tangent matrix $S(t)=D_\theta u_\theta(t)|_{\theta=\theta_0}$ is the unique solution of
$$S'(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)S(t)+D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0),\qquad S(0)=D u_0(\theta_0).$$
The result is local to the stated common compact tube and claims no differentiability outside it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open domain, $C^1$ field, parameter neighborhood, $C^1$ initial map, common bounded convex tube with compact closure in $D$, and the stated IVP solutions.

[F1] A first-order IVP solution satisfies its Volterra equation ([[prop-first-order-ivp-is-equivalent-to-a-volterra-integral-equation]]).

[F2] A uniform bound on the derivative over a convex open set gives the corresponding Lipschitz bound ([[thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F3] If $g(t)\le A+L\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ for nonnegative continuous $g$, then $g(t)\le A e^{Lt}$ ([[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]).

[F4] The norm of a vector-valued integral is at most the integral of its norm ([[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]]).

[F5] A continuous coefficient matrix on a compact interval gives a unique global solution of its linear matrix IVP ([[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]).

[A1] The parameter neighborhood and convex tube $O$ ensure all secant segments used below remain in $O$. Continuity of $D f$ on the compact closure $\overline O$ makes $D f$ bounded and uniformly continuous there.

## Proof

1.1 Let $\delta_h(t)=u_{\theta_0+h}(t)-u_{\theta_0}(t)$. Differentiability of $u_0$ gives $\|u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)\|_2\le C_0\|h\|_2$ for small $h$. Subtract the Volterra equations [F1] and apply [F2] on the segment between $(u_{\theta_0+h}(t),\theta_0+h)$ and $(u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. Boundedness of $D f$ on $O$ gives $$\|\delta_h(t)\|_2\le C_0\|h\|_2+L\int_0^t(\|\delta_h(s)\|_2+\|h\|_2)\,ds.$$ Since $t\le T$, [F3] yields $\sup_t\|\delta_h(t)\|_2\le(C_0+LT)e^{LT}\|h\|_2$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, A1, given]

1.2 Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and let $B_j(t)$ be column $j$ of $D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$. For each parameter coordinate $j$, the augmented vector $Z_j=(S_{\cdot j},1)$ solves the homogeneous linear system $$Z_j'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}A(t)&B_j(t)\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Z_j(t),\qquad Z_j(0)=\begin{pmatrix}D u_0(\theta_0)_{\cdot j}\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Embed $Z_j(0)$ as one column of a square $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ initial matrix, with all other columns zero. The unique linear matrix solution supplied by [F5] has that vector solution as the selected column. Thus the tangent equation has a unique solution for each of the finitely many columns. [A1, F5, construct]

2.1 Put $A(t)=D_u f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$ and $B(t)=D_\theta f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)$, and define $\rho_h(t)=f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t)+\delta_h(t),\theta_0+h)-f(t,u_{\theta_0}(t),\theta_0)-A(t)\delta_h(t)-B(t)h$. Uniform continuity of $D f$ on $\overline O$ and the integral remainder along the secant give $\sup_t\|\rho_h(t)\|_2=o(\|h\|_2)$, since step 1.1 gives $\sup_t(\|\delta_h(t)\|_2+\|h\|_2)=O(\|h\|_2)$. Also $u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)=D u_0(\theta_0)h+o(\|h\|_2)$. [A1, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $E_h(t)=\delta_h(t)-S(t)h$, and let $r_0(h)=u_0(\theta_0+h)-u_0(\theta_0)-D u_0(\theta_0)h$. The Volterra equations and the field remainder $\rho_h$ from step 2.1 give $E_h(t)=r_0(h)+\int_0^t\bigl(A(s)E_h(s)+\rho_h(s)\bigr)ds$, where $A(s)=D_u f(s,u_{\theta_0}(s),\theta_0)$. By [F4], $\|E_h(t)\|_2\le\|r_0(h)\|_2+T\sup_s\|\rho_h(s)\|_2+L\int_0^t\|E_h(s)\|_2ds$. Both first terms are $o(\|h\|_2)$ by step 2.1 and differentiability of $u_0$. Applying [F3] yields $\sup_t\|E_h(t)\|_2=o(\|h\|_2)$. Thus the Fréchet derivative at $\theta_0$ exists and equals $S$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 For any sequence $\theta_j\to\theta_0$ in $V_\theta$, step 1.1 gives $u_{\theta_j}\to u_{\theta_0}$ uniformly, and uniform continuity of $D f$ on $\overline O$ makes the tangent coefficients $A_j,B_j$ converge uniformly to $A,B$. Subtracting the tangent integral equations gives $S_j(t)-S(t)=D u_0(\theta_j)-D u_0(\theta_0)+\int_0^t\bigl(A_j(s)(S_j(s)-S(s))+(A_j(s)-A(s))S(s)+B_j(s)-B(s)\bigr)ds$. The initial and coefficient differences tend to zero, while $A_j$ are uniformly bounded; [F3] then gives $\|S_j-S\|_{C([0,T])}\to0$. Since $\theta_0$ is arbitrary in $V_\theta$, the derivative is continuous throughout that set, so the flow map is $C^1$. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $S\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^{d\times m})$ and $p\in C^1([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $S'=A S+B$ and $p'=-A^T p-g$, where $A,B,g$ are continuous and have compatible dimensions. Then
$$p(T)^T S(T)-p(0)^T S(0)=\int_0^T\bigl(-g(t)^T S(t)+p(t)^T B(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The continuously differentiable matrix and vector functions and their differential equations in the Statement.

[F1] The Euclidean pairing is the finite coordinate sum $x^Ty=\sum_i x_i y_i$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F2] The derivative of a product is $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F3] If $G'=q$ and $q$ is integrable on $[0,T]$, then $\int_0^Tq=G(T)-G(0)$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write $p^T S=\sum_{i=1}^d p_i S_{i,\cdot}$. By [F2] coordinatewise, $(p^TS)'=(p')^TS+p^TS'$. Substituting the two equations yields $(-A^Tp-g)^TS+p^T(AS+B)=-g^TS+p^TB$, because $(A^Tp)^TS=p^TAS$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The right-hand side in step 1.1 is continuous and hence integrable. Apply [F3] to the scalar function $p^TS$ and integrate step 1.1 over $[0,T]$. This gives the stated endpoint identity. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Use the setting of [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]. Write $A_n=D_x\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, $B_n=D_\theta\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$, and let $S_n=D_\theta x_n$. Then
$$S_0=D x_0(\theta),\qquad S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n.$$
Define $p_N=D_x\phi(x_N,\theta)^T$ and, backward for $n=N-1,\ldots,0$,
$$p_n=D_x\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+A_n^Tp_{n+1}.$$
The exact gradient of the finite objective is
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(x_N,\theta)^T+S_0^Tp_0+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\bigl(D_\theta\ell_n(x_n,\theta)^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}\bigr).$$
The recursion is the reverse derivative of the finite graph in exact real arithmetic; it makes no convergence claim about an iteration used to choose $\theta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open finite state-step graph, its $C^1$ maps, objective, trajectory and parameter in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-parameterized-finite-state-step-objective]]: $x_{n+1}=\Psi_n(x_n,\theta)$ and $J=\phi(x_N,\theta)+\sum_{n<N}\ell_n(x_n,\theta)$ with all displayed maps $C^1$.

[F2] [[alg-reverse-mode-automatic-differentiation]]: reverse mode accumulates each primitive pullback $D_k\phi_j^T\bar z_j$ at every parent slot in reverse topological order.

[F3] [[thm-reverse-mode-computes-gradient]]: reverse mode returns the exact gradient of the finite $C^1$ real-arithmetic graph.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the derivative of a composition is the composition of its derivatives.

## Proof

1.1 By the chain rule [F4] applied to $x_{n+1}(\theta)=\Psi_n(x_n(\theta),\theta)$, $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$; differentiating the initial map gives $S_0=Dx_0(\theta)$. These are the forward tangent equations for this finite composition. [F1, F4]

1.2 Apply the reverse accumulation rule [F2] to the finite graph of states and objective summands in [F1]. The terminal contribution seeds $p_N=D_x\phi^T$; at each state node $x_n$, its local running-cost edge contributes $D_x\ell_n^T$, while its state-transition edge contributes $A_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Thus the accumulated state cotangent is exactly $p_n$ as defined in the Statement, and the direct parameter edges contribute $D_\theta\phi^T$ and $D_\theta\ell_n^T+B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. By [F3], reverse mode returns the exact derivative of this finite C1 graph. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Differentiate the objective in [F1] using the forward sensitivities in step 1.1. The chain rule gives $$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S_N^TD_x\phi^T+\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(D_\theta\ell_n^T+S_n^TD_x\ell_n^T).$$ This is the direct tangent expression, with all derivatives evaluated along the trajectory. [F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 The adjoint equation gives $p_n^TS_n=D_x\ell_nS_n+p_{n+1}^TA_nS_n$. Since $S_{n+1}=A_nS_n+B_n$, rearranging yields $$D_x\ell_nS_n=p_n^TS_n-p_{n+1}^TS_{n+1}+p_{n+1}^TB_n.$$ Summing over $n$ telescopes; $p_N=D_x\phi^T$ cancels the terminal tangent term in step 2.1 and leaves $S_0^Tp_0+\sum_n B_n^Tp_{n+1}$. Adding the direct parameter derivatives from step 2.1 gives the displayed adjoint formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+D_\theta u_0(\theta)^Tp(0)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The common-tube ODE, $C^1$ initial map, objective, and bounded uniformly continuous first derivatives in the Statement.

[F1] [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]]: the parameter flow is $C^1$ and $S'=D_uf\,S+D_\theta f$, $S(0)=D_\theta u_0$.

[F2] [[lem-ode-adjoint-pairing-integration-by-parts]]: if $S'=AS+B$ and $p'=-A^Tp-g$, then $p(T)^TS(T)-p(0)^TS(0)=\int_0^T(-g^TS+p^TB)\,dt$.

[F3] [[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]: a continuous coefficient linear matrix IVP has a unique solution on the full compact interval.

[A1] All objective derivatives and ODE derivative coefficients are continuous and bounded on the common compact tube, and their first derivatives have the uniform continuity needed to differentiate the integral objective.

## Proof

1.1 By [F3], the terminal linear adjoint equation has a unique $C^1$ solution on $[0,T]$. [F3, given]

1.2 By [F1], the state depends $C^1$ on the parameter and has sensitivity $S$. The chain rule gives the column gradient of the running integrand as $D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+S(t)^TD_u\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T$. The mean-value integral formula, boundedness and uniform continuity of the objective derivatives on the common compact tube, and the uniform first-order state remainder from [F1] make the running first-order remainder $o(\|h\|)$ uniformly in $t$ for a parameter increment $h$. Integration therefore gives its derivative by integrating that column gradient. The terminal chain rule gives $D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T$. Consequently $\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T+\int_0^T(D_\theta\ell^T+S^TD_u\ell^T)\,dt$. [F1, A1, given]

1.3 In [F2], set $A=D_uf$, $B=D_\theta f$, and $g=D_u\ell^T$. The adjoint equation in the Statement and tangent equation in [F1] satisfy its hypotheses. Transposing that row pairing identity and using $p(T)=D_u\phi^T$ gives $$S(T)^TD_u\phi^T-D_\theta u_0^Tp(0)=\int_0^T(-S^TD_u\ell^T+D_\theta f^Tp)\,dt.$$ [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Substitute step 1.3 into step 1.2; the terms involving $S^TD_u\ell^T$ cancel, leaving the asserted continuous adjoint gradient formula. [step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $J$ and $J_h$ be the continuous and finite state-step objectives of [[thm-continuous-ode-adjoint-gradient-formula]] and [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]], respectively, and put $h=T/N$. Let $q(t,u,p)=D_\theta\ell(t,u,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u,\theta)^Tp$ be the continuous running-gradient vector, evaluated on its exact state and adjoint as $q(t):=q(t,u(t),p(t))$. Suppose the exact and numerical state/adjoint pairs lie in a common tube and
$$\max_n\bigl(\|u_n-u(t_n)\|_2+\|p_n-p(t_n)\|_2\bigr)\le C_xh^p.$$
For the state part of this bound, it is sufficient that the hypotheses of [[thm-global-error-from-one-step-defect-and-stability]] hold with a uniform $O(h^{p+1})$ exact-start defect; the coefficient conditions of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]] supply that defect for an explicit Runge--Kutta method of order $p\le4$ under that item's $C^4$ and common-tube assumptions. No cited state-error result supplies the adjoint part, which is an independent hypothesis here. Write $b$ and $b_h$ for the column initial/terminal contribution vectors in the continuous and discrete gradient formulas. Assume the discrete running-gradient terms admit vectors $\widehat q_n$ and nonnegative weights $w_n$, $0\le n\le N$, with
$$\nabla J_h=b_h+\sum_{n=0}^N w_n\widehat q_n,\qquad \nabla J=b+\int_0^Tq(t)\,dt,\qquad \sum_{n=0}^Nw_n=T.$$
The weighted discrete representation is an explicit premise; it is not implied by the generic finite state-step adjoint recursion. Suppose
$$\|\widehat q_n-q(t_n,u_n,p_n)\|_2\le C_dh^p,\qquad \|b_h-b\|_2\le C_bh^p,$$
and that the same weights give the quadrature $Q_h(q)=\sum_{n=0}^Nw_nq(t_n)$ satisfying
$$\left\|Q_h(q)-\int_0^Tq(t)\,dt\right\|_2\le C_Qh^p.$$
If $q$ is Lipschitz in $(u,p)$ on the common tube with constant $L_q$ in the sum norm, then
$$\|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|_2\le\bigl(C_b+T(C_d+L_qC_x)+C_Q\bigr)h^p.$$
The adjoint, derivative-data and quadrature hypotheses are separate from state accuracy; without them the state estimate alone gives no gradient error conclusion.

There is also the following independent method-consistency conclusion. Under the local $C^1$ step-and-cost consistency, derivative stability, derivative Lipschitz, initial-data, terminal-derivative and tube hypotheses of [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]], the actual numerical graph satisfies
$$\max_n\|D_\theta u_n-D_\theta u(t_n)\|_2\le C_Sh^p,\qquad \max_n\|p_n-p(t_n)\|_2\le C_Ph^p,$$
$$\|\nabla J_h-\nabla J\|_2\le C_Gh^p,$$
with that lemma's explicit constants, together with its state bound. These conclusions derive the global tangent and adjoint errors from local map errors. They do not assume the preceding global state/adjoint bound or weighted representation.

In particular, [[lem-explicit-rk-differentiated-stages-give-local-c1-order]] supplies these local hypotheses for the actual explicit RK state map and the cost using the same tableau, under its common-tube, base $C^2$, and local augmented-order hypotheses. For $p\le4$, its augmented $C^4$ hypothesis and the existing coefficient conditions suffice; jointly $C^5$ base data are an explicit sufficient smoothness condition, and its displayed classical RK4 tableau gives a concrete order-four instance. Generic $p$ is retained through its genuine local augmented-order hypothesis. This branch permits negative or zero RK weights and makes no internal-stage adjoint accuracy claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** In the weighted conclusion, the stated continuous and discrete objectives, exact adjoint formulas, uniform state/adjoint error bound, derivative-data perturbation bound, quadrature bound, and common compact tube. In the method-consistency conclusion, the actual step and cost maps and the separate local hypotheses of the two cited local lemmas.

[F1] [[thm-continuous-ode-adjoint-gradient-formula]]: the continuous gradient is the initial/terminal contribution plus $\int_0^T q(t)\,dt$.

[F2] [[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]: the discrete gradient is the corresponding initial/terminal contribution plus the reverse-mode sum of the discrete running derivative terms.

[F3] [[thm-global-error-from-one-step-defect-and-stability]]: the common-tube, uniform local-defect, one-step stability and initial-error hypotheses imply the stated uniform state-error bound.

[F4] [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]]: for an explicit tableau satisfying the stated coefficient equations through $p\le4$, a $C^4$ vector field on the common compact tube has uniform exact-start defect $O(h^{p+1})$. It supplies a state local-defect premise only when applied just to the state field; it makes no adjoint or tangent error claim by itself.

[F5] [[lem-local-c1-step-consistency-implies-tangent-adjoint-gradient-order]] derives global state, actual tangent, nodal-adjoint and gradient errors by comparing the exact-flow and numerical graphs under its local value/first-derivative hypotheses.

[F6] [[lem-explicit-rk-differentiated-stages-give-local-c1-order]] identifies derivatives of actual RK stages and matching cost quadrature with the same augmented method, verifies the local hypotheses of [F5], and instantiates local augmented order through four using [F4] on the augmented field.

[A1] For the weighted conclusion, the constants $C_b,C_x,C_d,C_Q,L_q$ are independent of $h$, and all error, quadrature and derivative-data hypotheses in that part of the Statement hold.

[A2] For the independent method-consistency conclusion, every hypothesis of [F5] holds, or is supplied by [F6] together with the initial and terminal hypotheses of [F5]. No global adjoint-error estimate is included in [A2].

## Proof

1.1 If the stated explicit Runge--Kutta conditions are used for the state field, [F4] supplies the exact-start defect required by [F3]. Under the stated stability, common-tube and initial-error hypotheses, [F3] gives the state part of the asserted $C_xh^p$ bound; the adjoint part in the weighted conclusion remains the separately assumed bound. [F3, F4, A1]

1.2 Independently assume [A2]. Apply [F5] to the actual maps defining $J_h$ and the exact interval flow and running-cost maps defining $J$. Its forward recurrences give state and tangent errors, its backward recurrence gives the nodal-adjoint error, and its graph-gradient comparison gives the stated $C_Gh^p$ bound. This argument uses no weighted decomposition. [A2, F5]

2.1 By [F1], [F2], and the explicit weighted representation in the Statement, the two gradients are their respective endpoint terms plus, respectively, the weighted sum of $\widehat q_n$ and the integral of $q$. At each node, insert and subtract $q(t_n,u_n,p_n)$. The derivative-data assumption and Lipschitz bound give $\|\widehat q_n-q(t_n)\|_2\le(C_d+L_qC_x)h^p$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $w_n\ge0$ and $\sum_nw_n=T$, the node-data perturbation contributes at most $T(C_d+L_qC_x)h^p$. The exact-integrand quadrature error contributes at most $C_Qh^p$, and the endpoint difference at most $C_bh^p$. The Euclidean triangle inequality gives the displayed weighted bound. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For the RK specialization, [F6] differentiates the actual finite stages, proves the local derivative-size and Lipschitz bounds, and obtains the needed local $C^1$ consistency from augmented local order. Its application of [F4] to the augmented field verifies this order for $p\le4$ under the actual augmented smoothness and tube assumptions. Its RK4 coefficient calculation supplies the concrete fourth-order instance. Therefore step 1.2 applies. [A2, F4, F6, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Use the implicit Runge–Kutta residual $G(Y)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ from [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]] on a convex open neighborhood of an invariant stage ball. Suppose $F$ is $C^1$ there and $\|D_YF(Y)Z\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Z\|_{\infty,2}$ for every $Y$ in the ball and every block vector $Z$. If $q=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$, then $D_YG(Y)$ is invertible at every point of the selected stage branch. The contraction hypotheses of [[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]] provide existence and uniqueness of the root in that ball; this lemma supplies nonsingularity for implicit differentiation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-dimensional stage space, implicit Runge–Kutta residual, selected invariant ball, $C^1$ map $F$, derivative bound $L$ on the ball, and $q<1$.

[F1] The stage residual is $G(Y)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$; a selected stage root satisfies $G(Y)=0$ ([[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]]).

[F2] If $F$ is Lipschitz on the invariant ball with constant $L$ and $h\|A\|_\infty L<1$, the stage fixed-point map has a unique root on the prescribed branch ([[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]]).

[F3] A vector-valued function continuous on $[0,1]$, differentiable on $(0,1)$, and with Euclidean derivative norm at most $M$ has endpoint difference at most $M$ ([[thm-mean-value-inequality]]). The chain rule differentiates a $C^1$ map along a segment ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F4] For a linear map on a finite-dimensional vector space, $\dim V=\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T$ ([[thm-rank-nullity]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let $Y,W$ belong to the invariant ball. Its convexity puts $Y+t(W-Y)$ in the ball for $0\le t\le1$. For each block $i$, the curve $\gamma_i(t)=F_i(Y+t(W-Y))$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable inside because $F$ is $C^1$ on an open neighborhood. Its derivative obeys $$\|\gamma_i'(t)\|_2\le\|D_YF(Y+t(W-Y))(W-Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}.$$ Apply [F3] to each block and take the maximum. This gives $\|F(W)-F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|W-Y\|_{\infty,2}$ using only the derivative bound on the ball. Hence [F2] applies with its invariant-ball hypotheses and the selected root exists uniquely. [given, F2, F3]

1.2 Differentiating [F1] with respect to $Y$ gives $D_YG=I-h(A\otimes I_d)D_YF$. If $D_YG\,Z=0$, the block row-sum norm and the derivative bound imply $$\|Z\|_{\infty,2}\le h\|A\|_\infty L\|Z\|_{\infty,2}=q\|Z\|_{\infty,2}.$$ Since $q<1$, this forces $Z=0$; thus the square finite-dimensional map $D_YG$ has trivial kernel. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], a linear map on the stage space has rank equal to its dimension when its kernel has dimension zero. Therefore $D_YG$ is onto as well as one-to-one, hence invertible. This holds at every point of the prescribed branch ball. [F4, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $u=u(\theta)$ be $C^1$ and consider a selected $s$-stage Runge–Kutta branch for a $C^1$ parameter-dependent vector field $f(t,y,\theta)$. Let $F(Y,u,\theta)$ be the stack of its stage evaluations and
$$G(Y,u,\theta)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y,u,\theta).$$
Assume the branch is the unique root in the invariant ball of [[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]], and its stage derivative $G_Y$ obeys the hypotheses of [[lem-implicit-rk-stage-jacobian-nonsingular-on-branch]]. Then the branch $Y(\theta)$ is locally $C^1$ and
$$D_\theta Y=-G_Y^{-1}\bigl(G_uD_\theta u+G_\theta\bigr).$$
For the update $\Psi_h(u,\theta)=u+h(\mathbf1^T_b\otimes I_d)F(Y(\theta),u(\theta),\theta)$,
$$D_\theta\Psi_h=D_\theta u+h(b^T\otimes I_d)\bigl(F_YD_\theta Y+F_uD_\theta u+F_\theta\bigr).$$
These are exact derivatives of the selected algebraic stage branch. A finite-budget stage iteration is a different map and is not covered by this formula.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The selected implicit Runge–Kutta tableau, the $C^1$ field, the initial state map, the invariant stage branch and the stated Jacobian nonsingularity.

[F1] The stage residual is $G(Y,u,\theta)=Y-\mathbf1\otimes u-h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y,u,\theta)$, and the update uses the weighted stage evaluations ([[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]]).

[F2] The selected branch is uniquely defined in its invariant ball when the contraction and ball-invariance hypotheses hold ([[lem-small-step-implicit-rk-branch-and-residual-error]]).

[F3] If a $C^1$ residual has a zero and an invertible state-block Jacobian, it has a local $C^1$ solution branch with derivative $-R_z^{-1}R_\theta$ ([[thm-implicit-differentiation-forward-and-adjoint-formulas]]).

[F4] The residual Jacobian is invertible under the stated contraction derivative bound ([[lem-implicit-rk-stage-jacobian-nonsingular-on-branch]]).

[F5] The derivative of a composition is given by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[A1] The field and stage maps are $C^1$ on an open neighborhood of the selected branch, and $G_Y$ is evaluated on that branch.

## Proof

1.1 By [F2], the stated root exists on the selected ball, and [F4] makes $G_Y$ invertible there. Regard $R(\theta,Y)=G(Y,u(\theta),\theta)$. Its parameter derivative is $R_\theta=G_uD_\theta u+G_\theta$. Apply [F3] to obtain the local branch and the displayed formula for $D_\theta Y$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, A1]

2.1 The update is the finite composition of $u(\theta)$, $Y(\theta)$ and the $C^1$ stage evaluation map in [F1]. Apply [F5] and the product rule for the linear output map $h(\mathbf1_b^T\otimes I_d)$ to get the displayed derivative. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The calculation differentiates the exact equation $G(Y,u(\theta),\theta)=0$ on its selected branch. It contains no update of a finite stage solver, so no derivative of a stopped iteration is asserted. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]]. On an open neighborhood $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, suppose the same constants $M<\infty$ and $\alpha>0$ give boundedness and coercivity for every $a_\theta$, and $\theta\mapsto A_\theta$ and $\theta\mapsto\ell_\theta$ are operator-norm $C^1$. Then each state $u_\theta$ exists uniquely, the map $\theta\mapsto u_\theta\in V$ is $C^1$, and for each direction $\eta\in\mathbb R^m$ its derivative $w_\eta=D_\theta u_\theta[\eta]$ is the unique solution of
$$a_\theta(w_\eta,v)=D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](v)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,v)\qquad(v\in V).$$
Uniform coercivity is required on the parameter neighborhood; no differentiability conclusion is asserted at a loss of coercivity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a real Hilbert space, the uniformly bounded/coercive family, operator-norm $C^1$ data, and the variational state definition in [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]].

[F1] Lax–Milgram gives a unique variational solution and $\alpha\|u\|_V\le\|F\|_{V^*}$ for each bounded linear datum ([[thm-lax-milgram]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F2] Operator-norm $C^1$ data means the increments of $A_\theta$ and $\ell_\theta$ equal their first derivatives plus remainders whose norms are $o(\|h\|_2)$ ([[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]]).

[A1] The constants $M,\alpha$ are uniform on the open parameter neighborhood $\Theta_0$, with $\alpha>0$.

## Proof

1.1 For each $\theta\in\Theta_0$, apply [F1] to $a_\theta$ and $\ell_\theta$; this gives a unique $u_\theta$ and the bound $\|u_\theta\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\|\ell_\theta\|_{V^*}$. Since $\ell_\theta$ is continuous, these state norms are locally bounded in $\theta$. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 For sufficiently small $h$ with $\theta+h\in\Theta_0$, put $\delta u=u_{\theta+h}-u_\theta$, $\delta A=A_{\theta+h}-A_\theta$, and $\delta\ell=\ell_{\theta+h}-\ell_\theta$. Subtract the two variational equations to get $a_\theta(\delta u,v)=\delta\ell(v)-(\delta A\,u_{\theta+h})(v)$. Taking $v=\delta u$, using coercivity and the dual norm, and dividing by $\|\delta u\|_V$ when it is nonzero gives $\|\delta u\|_V\le\alpha^{-1}\bigl(\|\delta\ell\|_{V^*}+\|\delta A\|\,\|u_{\theta+h}\|_V\bigr)=O(\|h\|_2)$. The same bound is immediate when $\delta u=0$. Thus the state map is locally Lipschitz. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For each direction $h\in\mathbb R^m$, define $w_h$ by $a_\theta(w_h,v)=D\ell_\theta[h](v)-\bigl(DA_\theta[h]u_\theta\bigr)(v)$. The right side is a bounded linear functional, so [F1] gives a unique $w_h$. Uniqueness and linearity of the right side in $h$ show $h\mapsto w_h$ is linear. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Write $\delta\ell=D\ell_\theta[h]+r_\ell$ and $\delta A=DA_\theta[h]+r_A$, where $\|r_\ell\|+\|r_A\|=o(\|h\|_2)$ by [F2]. Subtract the equation for $w_h$ in step 2.2 from the state-difference equation in step 2.1. With $e_h=\delta u-w_h$, this gives $a_\theta(e_h,v)=r_\ell(v)-(r_Au_\theta)(v)-(DA_\theta[h]\delta u)(v)-(r_A\delta u)(v)$. The first two terms have dual norm $o(\|h\|_2)$; the last two have that order because $\|DA_\theta[h]\|=O(\|h\|_2)$, $\|r_A\|=o(\|h\|_2)$, and $\|\delta u\|_V=O(\|h\|_2)$ by step 2.1. Coercivity yields $\|e_h\|_V=o(\|h\|_2)$, proving Fréchet differentiability and the stated derivative equation. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The solution operator $A_\theta^{-1}:V^*\to V$ has norm at most $\alpha^{-1}$. For nearby $\theta,\widetilde\theta$, the identity $A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}-A_\theta^{-1} =A_{\widetilde\theta}^{-1}(A_\theta-A_{\widetilde\theta})A_\theta^{-1}$ shows its operator-norm continuity. The formula in step 2.2, together with continuity of $u_\theta$, $D A_\theta$, and $D\ell_\theta$, then shows $D_\theta u_\theta$ is continuous. Hence the state map is $C^1$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the elliptic state setting of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]] and [[lem-elliptic-state-map-c1-under-uniform-coercivity]]. Let $J:V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For a parameter $\theta$, let $p_\theta\in V$ solve the adjoint variational problem
$$a_\theta(v,p_\theta)=D_uJ(u_\theta,\theta)[v]\qquad(v\in V).$$
Then the reduced objective $j(\theta)=J(u_\theta,\theta)$ is $C^1$ and
$$D_\theta j(\theta)[\eta]=D_\theta J(u_\theta,\theta)[\eta]+D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](p_\theta)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,p_\theta).$$
No symmetry of $a_\theta$ is required; the adjoint uses the transposed variational form displayed above.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The uniformly coercive real variational state, its $C^1$ dependence, the $C^1$ objective, and Countable Choice.

[F1] The state derivative $w_\eta$ is the unique solution of $a_\theta(w_\eta,v)=D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](v)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,v)$ ([[lem-elliptic-state-map-c1-under-uniform-coercivity]]).

[F2] A bounded linear functional has a unique adjoint variational solution with $a_\theta(v,p)=G(v)$ under Countable Choice ([[thm-adjoint-problem-for-bounded-coercive-variational-forms]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F3] The derivative of a $C^1$ composition obeys the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[A1] $J$ and its first derivatives are continuous on the state/parameter neighborhood.

## Proof

1.1 The adjoint datum $D_uJ(u_\theta,\theta)$ is a bounded linear functional on $V$. By [F2], the adjoint $p_\theta$ exists uniquely, with the equation in the Statement. [F2, A1, given]

1.2 By the chain rule [F3] and the state differentiability in [F1], $$D_\theta j[\eta]=D_\theta J(u_\theta,\theta)[\eta]+D_uJ(u_\theta,\theta)[w_\eta].$$ Use the adjoint equation with $v=w_\eta$ to replace the second term by $a_\theta(w_\eta,p_\theta)$. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Use the state-sensitivity equation [F1] with test function $v=p_\theta$. It gives $a_\theta(w_\eta,p_\theta)=D_\theta\ell_\theta[\eta](p_\theta)-D_\theta a_\theta[\eta](u_\theta,p_\theta)$. [F1, step 1.2]

3.1 Substitute step 2.1 into step 1.2 to obtain the formula. The argument uses only the displayed adjoint equation, so it remains valid for a nonsymmetric coercive form. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the elliptic state/adjoint setting of [[thm-elliptic-adjoint-reduced-gradient]]. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be a finite-dimensional conforming space. Let $a_{\theta,h}$ and $\ell_{\theta,h}$ be operator-norm $C^1$ in $\theta$, uniformly coercive on $V_h$, and define the discrete state by $a_{\theta,h}(u_h,v_h)=\ell_{\theta,h}(v_h)$. Let $J_h:V_h\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $p_h\in V_h$ solve $a_{\theta,h}(v_h,p_h)=D_uJ_h(u_h,\theta)[v_h]$. Suppose the parameter derivatives of the discrete forms and loads have specified bounded extensions to $V$ that agree with their values on $V_h$. Let $u,p$ be the exact state and adjoint, and let $u_h,p_h\in V_h$ be their discrete counterparts, with certified energy bounds
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le E_u,\qquad \|p-p_h\|_V\le E_p.$$
For an exact conforming Galerkin solve these bounds may be supplied by [[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]]; for a conforming perturbed solve they may be supplied by [[thm-first-strang-lemma-for-conforming-perturbed-galerkin]], with all load, form, geometry and quadrature defects retained as in [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. Define exact and discrete reduced gradients by
$$g[\eta]=D_\theta J(u,\theta)[\eta]+\ell_\theta'[\eta](p)-a_\theta'[\eta](u,p),\qquad g_h[\eta]=D_\theta J_h(u_h,\theta)[\eta]+\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta](p_h)-a_{\theta,h}'[\eta](u_h,p_h).$$
Assume for $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ that $\|\ell_\theta'[\eta]\|_{V^*}\le M_\ell$, $\|a_\theta'[\eta]\|_{\mathcal L(V,V^*)}\le M_a$, the direct-objective defect satisfies $|D_\theta J_h(u_h,\theta)[\eta]-D_\theta J(u,\theta)[\eta]|\le\varepsilon_J$, and the derivative-data defects obey
$$\|\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta]-\ell_\theta'[\eta]\|_{V^*}\le\varepsilon_\ell,\qquad \|a_{\theta,h}'[\eta]-a_\theta'[\eta]\|_{\mathcal L(V,V^*)}\le\varepsilon_a.$$
Put $U_*=\max(\|u\|_V,\|u_h\|_V)$ and $P_*=\max(\|p\|_V,\|p_h\|_V)$. Then
$$\|g_h-g\|_{\Theta^*}\le\varepsilon_J+M_\ell E_p+\varepsilon_\ell P_*+M_a(E_uP_*+U_*E_p)+\varepsilon_aU_*P_*.$$
The derivative-data defects are separate obligations: ordinary state and adjoint Strang bounds do not by themselves bound derivative defects.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exact elliptic reduced-gradient formula, the conforming discrete state and adjoint equations, their energy error bounds $E_u,E_p$, and the derivative-data bounds in the Statement.

[F1] The reduced gradient is $J_\theta[\eta]+\ell_\theta'[\eta](p)-a_\theta'[\eta](u,p)$ ([[thm-elliptic-adjoint-reduced-gradient]]).

[F2] Céa's estimate bounds a conforming Galerkin error by $M/\alpha$ times its best energy approximation ([[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]]).

[F3] For conforming perturbed forms, the first Strang estimate includes best approximation and form/load defects; the variational-crime framework identifies geometry, data and quadrature contributions to those defects ([[thm-first-strang-lemma-for-conforming-perturbed-galerkin]], [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]).

[F4] The derivative of a C1 composition is given by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[A1] Both state and adjoint equations satisfy the hypotheses of either [F2] or [F3], with their own right-hand sides, defects, and coercivity constants. Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) is used through those suppliers.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F2] to an exact conforming Galerkin state and its adjoint, or [F3] to each conforming perturbed equation, using the transposed form $a^\dagger(v,w)=a(w,v)$ for the adjoint. Transposition preserves boundedness and coercivity constants. Under [A1], the resulting two bounds are $E_u,E_p$, with all applicable form and load defects, including geometry and quadrature contributions, retained as specified by [F3]. [A1, F2, F3]

1.2 Choose a basis of $V_h$. Coercivity makes the discrete state matrix $K_h(\theta)$ invertible, and its entries and the load coordinates are $C^1$. The identity $K_h(\theta+z)^{-1}-K_h(\theta)^{-1}=-K_h(\theta+z)^{-1}(K_h(\theta+z)-K_h(\theta))K_h(\theta)^{-1}$ shows that its inverse, and hence $u_h(\theta)$, is $C^1$. Differentiating the state equation gives $a_{\theta,h}(w_h,v_h)=\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta](v_h)-a_{\theta,h}'[\eta](u_h,v_h)$. By [F4], $D j_h[\eta]=J_{\theta,h}'[\eta]+D_uJ_h[w_h]$; use the discrete adjoint equation with $v_h=w_h$, then the differentiated state equation with $v_h=p_h$, to obtain the formula for $g_h$ in the Statement. The continuous formula is supplied by [F1]. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\eta$ with $\|\eta\|_2\le1$. Subtract the continuous and discrete formulas. The direct-objective term is bounded by $\varepsilon_J$. Add and subtract $\ell_{\theta,h}'[\eta](p_h)$; the load-derivative difference is at most $\varepsilon_\ell P_*+M_\ell E_p$. [F1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Add and subtract $a_\theta'[\eta](u_h,p_h)$. The derivative-form data defect contributes at most $\varepsilon_a U_*P_*$. The remaining state/adjoint perturbation is $$|a_\theta'[\eta](u_h-u,p_h)+a_\theta'[\eta](u,p_h-p)|\le M_a(E_uP_*+U_*E_p).$$ Thus for every unit $\eta$, $|g_h[\eta]-g[\eta]|$ is bounded by the displayed constant. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Taking the supremum over all $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ gives the asserted dual norm bound. The separate $\varepsilon$ terms show why state error alone does not certify a reduced-gradient error. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the Galerkin and adjoint hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-fe-gradient-error-in-energy-norms]]. Suppose the adjoint regularity and dual approximation assumptions of [[cor-aubin-nitsche-h-r-plus-s-rate-under-primal-and-dual-approximation]] hold separately for the state and adjoint equations, giving
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2}\le C_u h^{r+s},\qquad \|p-p_h\|_{L^2}\le C_p h^{r+s}$$
for $0<h\le1$, $r\ge1$, and $s\in(0,1]$. Assume the parameter derivative operators satisfy
$$|\ell_\theta'[\eta](v)|\le M_\ell^0\|\eta\|_2\|v\|_{L^2},\qquad |a_\theta'[\eta](v,w)|\le M_a^0\|\eta\|_2\|v\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^2}.$$
Assume the discrete derivative maps in [[thm-elliptic-fe-gradient-error-in-energy-norms]] have compatible $L^2$ extensions and constants $C_J,C_\ell,C_a$ independent of $h$ give, for every $\|\eta\|_2\le1$, a direct-objective derivative defect at most $C_Jh^{r+s}$, an $L^2$-dual load-derivative defect at most $C_\ell h^{r+s}$, and a bilinear derivative defect at most $C_ah^{r+s}\|v\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^2}$. Then the reduced-gradient error is $O(h^{r+s})$. This rate requires those extra $L^2$-bounded parameter derivative maps; the energy-norm result alone does not imply it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The energy-norm reduced-gradient setting, the stated dual regularity bounds for the state and adjoint, Countable Choice, and the displayed $L^2$ derivative bounds.

[F1] The Aubin–Nitsche estimate gives an $h^{r+s}$ $L^2$ error under its stated primal and dual approximation hypotheses ([[cor-aubin-nitsche-h-r-plus-s-rate-under-primal-and-dual-approximation]]).

[F2] The energy-norm reduced-gradient bound separates state error, adjoint error, and derivative-data defects ([[thm-elliptic-fe-gradient-error-in-energy-norms]]).

[A1] Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the dual regularity and interpolation hypotheses hold separately for the continuous and adjoint Galerkin equations, with the constants displayed in the Statement; derivative-data and direct-objective defects are $O(h^{r+s})$ in the stated $L^2$ operator norms.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the state equation and to the adjoint equation with the transposed coercive form. Under [A1], this yields the two displayed $L^2$ error bounds. Countable Choice is required by [F1]. [F1, A1, given]

2.1 The parameter-derivative bounds in the Statement give $|\ell_\theta'[\eta](p_h-p)|\le M_\ell^0\|\eta\|_2 C_p h^{r+s}$ and, by adding and subtracting $a_\theta'[\eta](u,p_h)$, $|a_\theta'[\eta](u_h,p_h)-a_\theta'[\eta](u,p)|\le M_a^0\|\eta\|_2\bigl(C_u h^{r+s}\|p_h\|_{L^2}+\|u\|_{L^2}C_p h^{r+s}\bigr)$. The $L^2$ norms of $u$ and $p_h$ are bounded by the stated state bounds and $\|p_h\|_{L^2}\le\|p\|_{L^2}+C_ph^{r+s}$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply the exact gradient subtraction in [F2]. The direct-objective and derivative-data defects contribute their assumed $O(h^{r+s})$ bounds; step 2.1 bounds the state- and adjoint-dependent terms by constants times $h^{r+s}$. Taking the supremum over $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ proves the asserted rate. If the $L^2$ derivative bounds or either dual approximation hypothesis fails, this rate has not been proved. [A1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, and use the real evolution triple $(V,H,V^*)$ of [[def-parameterized-parabolic-variational-problem]]. On an open parameter set $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, assume the state map $\theta\mapsto u_\theta$ is Fr\'echet differentiable into $W(0,T;V)$, with derivative $w_\eta$ in direction $\eta\in\mathbb R^m$. Assume, for every $v\in V$ and almost every $t$,
$$\langle w_\eta'(t),v\rangle+a_\theta(t;w_\eta(t),v)=\langle f_\theta'[\eta](t),v\rangle-a_\theta'[\eta](t;u_\theta(t),v),\qquad w_\eta(0)=u_{0,\theta}'[\eta].$$
Let $\phi:H\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $L:[0,T]\times V\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be measurable in time and $C^1$ in $(u,\theta)$ for almost every time, with a common integrable majorant that justifies differentiating its time integral. Assume $D_u\phi$ is represented by an element of $H$ and $D_uL(t,u_\theta,\theta)\in V^*$ is square-integrable in time. Suppose the adjoint $p\in W(0,T;V)$ satisfies
$$-\langle p'(t),v\rangle+a_\theta(t;v,p(t))=D_uL(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)[v],\qquad p(T)=\nabla_H\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta).$$
Then for $j(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T L(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt$,
$$D j(\theta)[\eta]=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)[\eta]+(p(0),u_{0,\theta}'[\eta])_H+\int_0^T\left(D_\theta L(t,u_\theta,\theta)[\eta]+\langle f_\theta'[\eta](t),p(t)\rangle-a_\theta'[\eta](t;u_\theta(t),p(t))\right)dt.$$
This is conditional on the displayed differentiable state and adjoint; it does not prove either exists. The adjoint form is transposed as shown, so symmetry of $a_\theta$ is not required.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The real evolution triple, differentiable parameterized state and objective, its linearized equation, and a solution of the stated terminal adjoint equation.

[F1] The parameterized parabolic state and reduced objective use the variational equation on $W(0,T;V)$ with $H$ traces ([[def-parameterized-parabolic-variational-problem]]).

[F2] For $w,p\in W(0,T;V)$, the evolution-space pairing identity is $(p(T),w(T))_H-(p(0),w(0))_H=\int_0^T(\langle p',w\rangle+\langle w',p\rangle)dt$ ([[lem-parabolic-energy-pairing-and-trace]]).

[F3] Differentiable compositions and sums obey the Banach-space chain rule ([[thm-chain-sum-product-and-composition-rules-for-banach-derivatives]]).

[A1] Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) is required by the pairing supplier ([[lem-parabolic-energy-pairing-and-trace]]). No use is made of a parabolic well-posedness theorem to infer state or adjoint existence.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F3] to the terminal term and the running integrand. The common integrable majorant permits differentiation under the integral, so $$D j[\eta]=D_\theta\phi[\eta]+(\nabla_H\phi,w_\eta(T))_H+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta L[\eta]+D_uL[w_\eta]\bigr)dt.$$ The terminal condition replaces $\nabla_H\phi$ by $p(T)$. [F1, F3, given]

1.2 Apply [F2] to $w_\eta$ and $p$. By the adjoint equation with $v=w_\eta$ and the linearized state equation with $v=p$, the integrand in its right side is $$\langle p',w_\eta\rangle+\langle w_\eta',p\rangle=a_\theta(t;w_\eta,p)-D_uL[w_\eta]+\langle f_\theta'[\eta],p\rangle-a_\theta(t;w_\eta,p)-a_\theta'[\eta](u_\theta,p),$$ so the two terms containing $a_\theta(t;w_\eta,p)$ cancel. Countable Choice enters here through the pairing result [F2]. [A1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The pairing identity now gives $(p(T),w_\eta(T))_H=(p(0),u_{0,\theta}'[\eta])_H+\int_0^T(-D_uL[w_\eta]+\langle f_\theta'[\eta],p\rangle-a_\theta'[\eta](u_\theta,p))dt$. Substitute this into step 1.1; the terms $D_uL[w_\eta]$ cancel and yield the displayed formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the differentiable state/adjoint setting of [[thm-parabolic-adjoint-gradient-sensitivity]]. Let $u,p$ and $u_h,p_h$ denote the continuous and semidiscrete state/adjoint pairs, with gradients $g,g_h$ given by that theorem and its finite-dimensional application. Assume $u,p\in H^1(0,T;V)$, the parabolic form and its parameter derivative are uniformly bounded, and the form is coercive with constant $\alpha>0$. Suppose the forward state and time-reversed adjoint both satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-parabolic-semidiscrete-ritz-error-splitting-and-energy-bound]], with operator-norm $C^1$ comparison maps $P_{u,h}(t),P_{p,h}(t):V\to V_h$. For the state comparison map, set $\rho_u=P_{u,h}u-u$, $\vartheta_u=u_h-P_{u,h}u$, and
$$\mathcal R_u(t)(v_h)=(\rho_u'(t),v_h)_H+a_\theta(t;\rho_u(t),v_h),\qquad \rho_u'=P_{u,h}'(t)u+P_{u,h}(t)u'-u'.$$
In reverse time $s=T-t$, put $q(s)=p(T-s)$ and $\widetilde P_{p,h}(s)=P_{p,h}(T-s)$; define $\rho_p(s)=\widetilde P_{p,h}(s)q(s)-q(s)$, $\vartheta_p(s)=p_h(T-s)-\widetilde P_{p,h}(s)q(s)$, and $\mathcal R_p(s)(v_h)=(\rho_p'(s),v_h)_H+a_\theta(T-s;v_h,\rho_p(s))$. The projection product rule gives $\rho_p'=\widetilde P_{p,h}'q+\widetilde P_{p,h}q'-q'$, with $\widetilde P_{p,h}'(s)=-P_{p,h}'(T-s)$. The Ritz supplier gives, for $z=u,p$,
$$\|z-z_h\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}\le E_z:=\|\rho_z\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}+\alpha^{-1/2}\left(\|\vartheta_z(0)\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\|\mathcal R_z\|_{L^2(0,T;V_h^*)}^2\right)^{1/2},$$
where the adjoint's initial trace means its terminal trace in original time. In particular, $\mathcal R_z$ contains the derivative of the time-dependent projection; it cannot be dropped from this hypothesis.

For $\|\eta\|_2\le1$, assume $\|D_\theta f[\eta]\|_{L^2(V^*)}\le M_f$, $\|D_\theta a(t)[\eta]\|_{\mathcal L(V,V^*)}\le M_a$ a.e., and define $U_*:=\max(\|u\|_{L^2(V)},\|u_h\|_{L^2(V)})$, $P_*:=\max(\|p\|_{L^2(V)},\|p_h\|_{L^2(V)})$, $P_{0,*}:=\max(\|p(0)\|_H,\|p_h(0)\|_H)$, and $U_0':=\|D_\theta u_0\|_{\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m,H)}$. Suppose the discrete direct-objective derivative differs from the continuous direct-objective derivative $D_\theta\phi+\int_0^T D_\theta L\,dt$ by at most $\varepsilon_J$ in $\Theta^*$; suppose also $\|D_\theta u_{0,h}-D_\theta u_0\|_{\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m,H)}\le\varepsilon_0$, $\|D_\theta f_h-D_\theta f\|_{\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m,L^2(V^*))}\le\varepsilon_f$, and $\|D_\theta a_h-D_\theta a\|_{L^\infty(0,T;\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal L(V,V^*)))}\le\varepsilon_a$. Put $E_{p,0}=\|p_h(0)-p(0)\|_H$. Then
$$\|g_h-g\|_{(\mathbb R^m)^*}\le \varepsilon_J+U_0'E_{p,0}+P_{0,*}\varepsilon_0+M_fE_p+\varepsilon_fP_*+M_a(E_uP_*+U_*E_p)+\varepsilon_aU_*P_*.$$
The derivative-data and trace defects are additional assumptions; an energy estimate for the state alone does not imply this gradient bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The continuous and semidiscrete differentiable state/adjoint pairs, their objective-gradient formulas, the bounded coercive form, parameter derivative bounds, and the time-dependent Ritz comparison maps and residuals.

[F1] The parabolic adjoint formula expresses the gradient through the initial trace, forcing derivative, bilinear-form derivative and direct objective terms ([[thm-parabolic-adjoint-gradient-sensitivity]]).

[F2] The Ritz splitting obeys the residual identity and energy estimate, and for a time-dependent comparison map its residual uses $\rho'=P_h'u+P_hu'-u'$ ([[thm-parabolic-semidiscrete-ritz-error-splitting-and-energy-bound]]).

[F3] The weak time product rule yields $(P_h(t)u(t))'=P_h'(t)u(t)+P_h(t)u'(t)$ for an operator-norm $C^1$ family ([[lem-parabolic-projection-time-product-rule]]).

[A1] Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) is required by the cited parabolic energy/pairing results. Both state and time-reversed transposed adjoint estimates, all traces, and all displayed derivative-data defects are assumed to satisfy their stated hypotheses ([[thm-parabolic-semidiscrete-ritz-error-splitting-and-energy-bound]], [[lem-parabolic-energy-pairing-and-trace]]).

## Proof

1.1 For the forward state, the product rule [F3] gives $\rho_u'=P_{u,h}'u+P_{u,h}u'-u'$, so the residual in [F2] is exactly the one displayed in the Statement. Apply the energy estimate in [F2] to $\vartheta_u$; it gives $\|\vartheta_u\|_{L^2(V)}\le\alpha^{-1/2}(\|\vartheta_u(0)\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\|\mathcal R_u\|_{L^2(V_h^*)}^2)^{1/2}$. Since $u-u_h=-\rho_u-\vartheta_u$, the triangle inequality proves the stated $E_u$ bound. [A1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Set $s=T-t$ and $q(s)=p(T-s)$. The backward adjoint equation becomes a forward parabolic variational equation with transposed form $a_\theta(T-s;v,w)$, which has the same boundedness and coercivity constants. The comparison $\widetilde P_{p,h}(s)=P_{p,h}(T-s)$ is operator-norm $C^1$ and $\widetilde P_{p,h}'(s)=-P_{p,h}'(T-s)$. By [F3], its residual contains $\widetilde P_{p,h}'q+\widetilde P_{p,h}q'-q'$; apply the energy estimate in [F2] and the splitting $p-p_h=-\rho_p-\vartheta_p$ to get the stated $E_p$ bound by the same triangle inequality as step 1.1. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Subtract the two gradient formulas [F1]. The direct term contributes $\varepsilon_J$. For the initial pairing, add and subtract $(p_h(0),D_\theta u_0)$; Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the difference by $U_0'E_{p,0}+P_{0,*}\varepsilon_0$. In the forcing term, add and subtract $D_\theta f[p_h]$; the derivative-data defect is at most $\varepsilon_fP_*$, and the exact derivative contributes at most $M_fE_p$ by step 2.1. Thus the direct, initial, and forcing contributions are bounded by the first four terms in the stated gradient estimate. [A1, F1, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 For the form term, add and subtract $D_\theta a[u_h,p_h]$. Its derivative-data defect is at most $\varepsilon_aU_*P_*$. Split the exact derivative difference as $D_\theta a[u_h-u,p_h]+D_\theta a[u,p_h-p]$; Cauchy--Schwarz in time, the bound $\|D_\theta a[\eta]\|\le M_a$, and steps 1.1 and 2.1 give $M_a(E_uP_*+U_*E_p)$. Combine this with step 3.1 and take the supremum over $\|\eta\|_2\le1$ to obtain the displayed dual norm bound. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A_1,\ldots,A_N\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be invertible, with $n,N\ge1$, and let $Q_0$ be orthogonal. For $1\le k\le N$, form the unique positive-diagonal QR factorization
$$A_kQ_{k-1}=Q_kR_k,$$
where $Q_k$ is orthogonal and $R_k$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal $r_{k,ii}$. Put $P_N=A_N\cdots A_1$ and define the exact finite-time log-volume change by $\log|\det P_N|$. Then
$$\log|\det P_N|=\sum_{k=1}^N\sum_{i=1}^n\log r_{k,ii}.$$
No infinite-time Lyapunov exponent or shadowing conclusion follows.

For a numerical log record, define $\sigma_{\min}(A):=\inf_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Ax\|_2$. If $\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma>0$, each exact $r_{k,ii}\ge\sigma$. If positive computed diagonals $\widetilde r_{k,ii}$ satisfy $|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|\le\varepsilon_{k,i}\le\sigma/2$, and each computed logarithm $\widehat l_{k,i}$ satisfies $|\widehat l_{k,i}-\log\widetilde r_{k,ii}|\le\delta_{k,i}$, then
$$\left|\sum_{k,i}\widehat l_{k,i}-\log|\det P_N|\right|\le\sum_{k,i}\left(\frac{2\varepsilon_{k,i}}{\sigma}+\delta_{k,i}\right).$$
If any factor loses rank, this log-volume branch returns failure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite list of invertible tangent matrices, an orthogonal $Q_0$, and the stated factorizations. The numerical bound additionally assumes the displayed certified singular-value and log-evaluation errors.

[F1] Every invertible real square matrix has a unique factorization $A=QR$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $R$ upper triangular with positive diagonal ([[thm-qr-factorisation-over-r-or-c]]).

[F2] Determinants multiply under finite square matrix products ([[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]).

[F3] The determinant of an upper triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries ([[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]).

[F4] An orthogonal matrix has determinant modulus one ([[cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus]]).

[F5] The logarithm difference is the integral of $1/t$ between positive endpoints ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]).

[A1] For the numerical bound, $\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma>0$, $|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|\le\varepsilon_{k,i}\le\sigma/2$, and the computed logarithm errors are bounded by $\delta_{k,i}$.

## Proof

1.1 Induction on $k$ using $A_kQ_{k-1}=Q_kR_k$ gives $$P_kQ_0=Q_kR_kR_{k-1}\cdots R_1,\qquad P_k:=A_k\cdots A_1.$$ For $k=1$ this is the defining factorization; multiplying the identity at $k$ on the left by $A_{k+1}$ and substituting $A_{k+1}Q_k=Q_{k+1}R_{k+1}$ proves the next case. [given, algebra, induction]

1.2 Orthogonal factors preserve Euclidean norms, so $\sigma_{\min}(R_k)=\sigma_{\min}(Q_kR_k)=\sigma_{\min}(A_kQ_{k-1})=\sigma_{\min}(A_k)\ge\sigma$. For a fixed $i$, the leading $(i-1)\times(i-1)$ block of $R_k$ is invertible. Choose $x\in\mathbb R^{i-1}$ solving $R_{1:i-1,1:i-1}x=-R_{1:i-1,i}$ and set $z=(x,1,0,\ldots,0)^T$. Upper triangularity gives $R_kz=r_{k,ii}e_i$ and $\|z\|_2\ge1$, so $\sigma_{\min}(R_k)\le\|R_kz\|_2/\|z\|_2\le r_{k,ii}$. For $i=1$, take $z=e_1$. Hence $r_{k,ii}\ge\sigma$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Take determinants in step 1.1. By [F2], $\det(P_N)\det(Q_0)=\det(Q_N)\prod_{k=1}^N\det(R_k)$. By [F3] each $\det(R_k)=\prod_i r_{k,ii}>0$, and by [F4] $|\det(Q_0)|=|\det(Q_N)|=1$. Thus $|\det(P_N)|=\prod_{k,i}r_{k,ii}$. Taking logarithms of positive numbers proves the exact identity. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Both $r_{k,ii}$ and $\widetilde r_{k,ii}$ are at least $\sigma/2$. By [F5], $|\log\widetilde r_{k,ii}-\log r_{k,ii}|\le(2/\sigma)|\widetilde r_{k,ii}-r_{k,ii}|$. Adding the computation error $\delta_{k,i}$ and summing the scalar bounds by the triangle inequality proves the stated numerical log bound. The lower singular-value bound is essential to keep the log derivative bounded; if any factor is singular its determinant is zero and its log-volume is undefined. [A1, F5, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $V=H_0^1(0,1)$ with its standard $H^1$ norm, let $\Theta=(-1,\infty)$, and define $a_\theta(u,v)=(1+\theta)\int_0^1u'v'\,dx$ and $\ell(v)=\int_0^1v\,dx$. Take $J(u)=\int_0^1u\,dx$. On a neighborhood of each fixed $\theta>-1$, the form is uniformly coercive in the $H^1$ norm, so this is a parameterized coercive elliptic problem in the sense of [[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-dimensional Sobolev space, the displayed bilinear form/load, and the reduced-gradient formula.

[F1] For a uniformly coercive parameterized elliptic variational state and $C^1$ objective, the adjoint formula gives $D_\theta j=D_\theta J+D_\theta\ell(p)-D_\theta a(u,p)$ ([[thm-elliptic-adjoint-reduced-gradient]]).

[F2] The elliptic variational definition treats states as weak solutions of $a_\theta(u,v)=\ell_\theta(v)$ ([[def-parameterized-elliptic-variational-problem]]).

[F3] The quadratic $w(x)=x(1-x)/2$ belongs to $H^1_0(0,1)$ ([[lem-two-cell-hat-and-quadratic-functions-lie-in-h10]]).

[F4] For $v\in H^1_0(0,1)$, $\|v\|_{H^1}\le\sqrt2\|v'\|_{L^2}$ ([[lem-one-dimensional-zero-boundary-poincare]]).

[F5] $H^1_0(0,1)$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(0,1)$ in the $H^1$ norm ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F6] The integral of the derivative of a C1 scalar function equals its endpoint increment ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

[F7] Differentiable products obey the product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F8] The integral pairing is bounded by the product of L2 norms ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]).

[A1] Countable Choice is inherited from the state, adjoint, and H0 membership suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Verification

1.1 Put $w(x)=x(1-x)/2$. Direct differentiation gives $w''=-1$, $w(0)=w(1)=0$, and [F3] gives $w\in V$. For each $v\in V$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F5] supplies $v_\varepsilon\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ with $\|v-v_\varepsilon\|_{H^1}<\varepsilon$. By the product rule [F7], $(w'v_\varepsilon)'=w''v_\varepsilon+w'v_\varepsilon'$; since $v_\varepsilon$ vanishes at both endpoints, [F6] gives $\int_0^1w'v_\varepsilon'=\int_0^1v_\varepsilon$. By [F8], the difference between the two sides with $v$ in place of $v_\varepsilon$ is at most $(\|w'\|_{L^2}+1)\varepsilon$, so the weak identity $\int_0^1w'v'=\int_0^1v$ follows as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Also, [F4] gives $a_\theta(v,v)\ge(1+\theta)\|v\|_{H^1}^2/2$; on a neighborhood of each $\theta>-1$ this is a uniform coercivity bound. Hence $u_\theta=w/(1+\theta)$ solves the state equation and is unique. Finally $\int_0^1w=1/12$, so $j(\theta)=1/(12(1+\theta))$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 The adjoint equation is $a_\theta(v,p)=D_uJ[v]=\int_0^1v$ for all $v\in V$, so symmetry of $a_\theta$ and uniqueness give $p=u_\theta$. The direct parameter derivatives of $J$ and $\ell$ vanish. For the scalar parameter direction $1$, $D_\theta a[1](u,p)=\int_0^1u'p'\,dx=(1+\theta)^{-2}\int_0^1(w')^2dx$. Direct integration gives $\int_0^1(w')^2dx=\frac14\int_0^1(1-2x)^2dx=1/12$, hence $D_\theta a[1](u,p)=1/(12(1+\theta)^2)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Formula [F1] therefore gives $j'(\theta)=-1/(12(1+\theta)^2)$, equal to the derivative of the explicit reduced objective in step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

For $u'=\theta u$ on two intervals of length $\tau>0$, define shooting nodes $z_0,z_1,z_2$ and residuals $R_0=z_0-a$, $R_1=z_1-e^{\tau\theta}z_0$, and $R_2=z_2-e^{\tau\theta}z_1$. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $a\in\mathbb R$, $\tau>0$, the two exact-flow intervals, and the finite shooting graph.

[F1] The parameterized ODE flow has its variational tangent when its uniqueness and common-tube hypotheses hold ([[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]]).

[F2] The reverse recursion computes the exact gradient of a finite state-step objective ([[thm-discrete-adjoint-gradient-recursion]]).

[F3] The exponential is smooth with derivative equal to itself, is positive, satisfies $e^{-x}=1/e^x$, and is increasing ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

[F4] The chain and product rules differentiate the displayed functions; a continuous function on an interval with zero interior derivative is constant ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]).

1.1 The function $u(t)=e^{\theta t}s$ satisfies $u'=\theta u$ and $u(0)=s$. Conversely, for any solution $v$ with this initial value, the product and chain rules give $(e^{-\theta t}v(t))'=0$. By [F4] this product is constantly $s$ on its solution interval, and positivity and the reciprocal identity in [F3] imply $v(t)=e^{\theta t}s$. Thus the displayed solution exists globally and is unique. [F3, F4]

2.1 Verify the actual common-tube hypotheses locally at any $(s_*,\theta_*)$. Fix $\varepsilon,\delta,\eta>0$ and restrict the parameters to $|s-s_*|<\varepsilon$, $|\theta-\theta_*|<\delta$. For $-\eta\le t\le\tau+\eta$, $$|e^{\theta t}s|\le B:=(|s_*|+\varepsilon)\exp((|\theta_*|+\delta)(\tau+\eta)).$$ Treat $(s,\theta)$ as the flow parameter, with initial map $(s,\theta)\mapsto s$ and field $(t,u,s,\theta)\mapsto\theta u$ on $\mathbb R^4$. The bounded convex open set $$(-\eta,\tau+\eta)\times(-B-1,B+1)\times(s_*-2\varepsilon,s_*+2\varepsilon)\times(\theta_*-2\delta,\theta_*+2\delta)$$ has compact closure inside that field's domain and contains all these trajectories for $0\le t\le\tau$ and the restricted parameters. The field and initial map are $C^1$. Step 1.1 supplies existence and uniqueness, so [F1] applies. Each shooting interval uses this same argument with its own initial node; since there are two intervals, a common finite bound may also be taken. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The exact interval map is therefore $\Phi_\tau(s,\theta)=e^{\tau\theta}s$. Differentiate the residuals with respect to $(z_0,z_1,z_2)$ and $\theta$, writing $E=e^{\tau\theta}$: $$D_zR=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\-E&1&0\\0&-E&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_\theta R=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-\tau E z_0\\-\tau E z_1\end{pmatrix}.$$ The state Jacobian is lower bidiagonal, and the parameter column contains the two local flow sensitivities. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Solving $R=0$ gives $z_0=a$, $z_1=Ea$, and $z_2=E^2a$. Direct differentiation yields $D_\theta z_2=2\tau E^2a$. Thus the reverse gradient agrees with the differentiated shooting solution. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Uniform convergence of approximate states to an exact state, by itself, implies convergence or a uniform bound for their parameter derivatives.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The displayed $C^1$ scalar maps and the uniform state norm on $(-1,1)$.

## Statement

Let $s\ge1$, let $R_1,\ldots,R_s$ be complex matrices of one fixed shape,
and let $C\ge1$. Define
$$\mathcal C_{s,C}:=\{c\in\mathbb R^s:\sum_{i=1}^s c_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|\le C\}$$
and $J(c):=\|\sum_{i=1}^s c_iR_i\|_F^2$. Then $J$ attains a minimum on
$\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Among all minimizers there is a unique vector of minimum
Euclidean norm. This rule defines the exact capped DIIS coefficient vector even
when the least-squares Gram matrix is singular.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A positive integer $s$, matrices $R_i$ of the same finite shape, and a real cap $C\ge1$.

[F1] The Frobenius norm is a norm on the finite-dimensional matrix space ([[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]).

[F2] A closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^s$ is compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F3] Real absolute values satisfy $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$ and $|ab|=|a||b|$ ([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]).

## Proof


1.1 The vector $e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ belongs to $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ because its entries sum to $1$ and its $\ell^1$ norm is $1\le C$. Thus the coefficient set is nonempty. It is closed: the sum constraint is the inverse image of the closed singleton $\{1\}$ under a continuous linear map, and the $\ell^1$ bound is the inverse image of the closed interval $(-\infty,C]$ under the continuous function $c\mapsto\sum_i|c_i|$. It is bounded because $\|c\|_1^2=\sum_i c_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}|c_i||c_j|\ge\|c\|_2^2$ and $\|c\|_1\le C$. Therefore [F2] makes $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ compact. [given, F2]

2.1 The map $c\mapsto\sum_i c_iR_i$ is linear and continuous in finite dimensions, and its squared Frobenius norm is continuous by [F1]. The extreme-value theorem gives a minimum; its minimizer set is closed as the inverse image of the singleton containing that minimum, hence compact as a closed subset of $\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Thus [F2] gives a nonempty compact set $M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal C_{s,C}}J(c)$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 For $c,d\in\mathcal C_{s,C}$ and $0\le t\le1$, the coefficients $e=(1-t)c+td$ satisfy $\sum_i e_i=(1-t)\sum_i c_i+t\sum_i d_i=1$. By [F3], $\sum_i|e_i|\le(1-t)\sum_i|c_i|+t\sum_i|d_i|\le C$, so $\mathcal C_{s,C}$ is convex. The set $M$ is also convex: for matrices $A,B$ the identity $\|(1-t)A+tB\|_F^2=(1-t)\|A\|_F^2+t\|B\|_F^2-t(1-t)\|A-B\|_F^2$ proves convexity of the squared norm. Applying it to $A=\sum_i c_iR_i$ and $B=\sum_i d_iR_i$ shows $J((1-t)c+td)\le(1-t)J(c)+tJ(d)=\min J$, so the convex combination also minimizes. Since $M$ is compact, the continuous function $c\mapsto\|c\|_2^2$ has a minimizer $c_*\in M$. [step 2.1, F1, F3, algebra]

4.1 If distinct $c,d\in M$ both had minimum Euclidean norm, their midpoint would lie in $M$ and satisfy $\left\|\frac{c+d}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2}-\frac{\|c-d\|_2^2}{4}<\frac{\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2}{2},$ contradicting minimality. Thus $c_*$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares minimizer. No nonsingularity of the Gram matrix is needed for existence or tie-breaking. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have eigenvalues with multiplicity
$\lambda_1(H_0)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H_0)$ and gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$. Put
$$c=\lambda_1(H_0),\qquad R=\frac{\lambda_r(H_0)+\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)}2-c,$$
and let $\Gamma=\{c+Re^{it}:0\le t\le2\pi\}$ be positively oriented.
For Hermitian $H$, write $\sigma(H)=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$.
Then
$R\ge g/2$. For every Hermitian $H$ with $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, exactly
the $r$ lowest eigenvalues of $H$, counted with multiplicity, lie inside $\Gamma$;
the gap is at least $g/2$, and
$$\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma,\sigma(H))\ge g/4,\qquad \|(zI-H)^{-1}\|_{op}\le4/g\quad(z\in\Gamma).$$

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A Hermitian $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$, integers $n\ge2$ and $1\le r<n$, and $g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$.

[F1] Descending ordered Hermitian eigenvalues change by at most the operator norm of the matrix perturbation ([[lem-complex-hermitian-eigenvalues-lipschitz]]); ascending order is obtained by reversing indices, so the same bound holds for the ascending convention used here.

[F2] A finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F3] The operator norm is the supremum of $\|Tv\|_2$ over unit vectors $v$ ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).

## Proof


1.1 Since $\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)=\lambda_r(H_0)+g$, we have $R=\lambda_r(H_0)-\lambda_1(H_0)+g/2\ge g/2>0$. Reversing the descending-index convention in [F1] gives the same perturbation bound for the ascending eigenvalues used here. Thus if $\|H-H_0\|_{op}\le g/4$, then $\lambda_1(H)\ge c-g/4$ and $\lambda_r(H)\le c+R-g/4$. Since $R-g/4\ge g/4$, every first-$r$ eigenvalue therefore satisfies $|\lambda_j(H)-c|\le R-g/4$, so it lies at least $g/4$ inside the circle centered at $c$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The same eigenvalue estimate gives $\lambda_{r+1}(H)\ge c+R+g/4$, so all remaining eigenvalues satisfy $|\lambda_j(H)-c|\ge R+g/4$ and lie at least $g/4$ outside the circle. Also $\lambda_{r+1}(H)-\lambda_r(H)\ge g-2(g/4)=g/2$. Thus the contour separates exactly the occupied cluster and the stated gap persists. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 By [F2], the spectrum of $H$ is real and $H$ diagonalizes unitarily. For every $z\in\Gamma$, reverse triangle gives $|z-\lambda_j(H)|\ge||z-c|-|\lambda_j(H)-c||\ge g/4$ by steps 1.1–1.2. In the unitary eigenbasis, $(zI-H)^{-1}$ is diagonal with entries of modulus at most $4/g$. Applying [F3] to a unit vector in this basis gives $\|(zI-H)^{-1}\|_{op}\le4/g$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every $X\in U$ at which the response map of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] has a strict $r$th gap,
$\Phi(X)$ is a uniquely defined member of $\mathcal P_r$. Degeneracies among
the first $r$ eigenvalues or among the remaining eigenvalues do not affect it.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A Hermitian matrix $F(X)$ with ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$ and $\lambda_r<\lambda_{r+1}$.

[F1] A finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F2] The response-map definition selects the sum of eigenspaces belonging to the $r$ lowest eigenvalues ([[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]]).

[L1] $\mathcal P_r=\{P=P^*:P^2=P,\operatorname{tr}P=r\}$ ([[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]).

[F3] The trace of a square matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]).

## Proof


1.1 By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $F(X)$ with the eigenvalues in the given order. The strict gap prevents an eigenspace for one eigenvalue from straddling positions $r$ and $r+1$, so the sum of the first $r$ eigenspaces is the span of exactly the first $r$ basis vectors. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Changing the orthonormal basis within a repeated eigenspace below the gap leaves that entire eigenspace in the sum; changing one within a repeated eigenspace above the gap leaves that entire eigenspace out. Thus the selected subspace does not depend on the eigenbasis chosen in step 1.1. Its orthogonal projector is $P=\sum_{j=1}^r u_ju_j^*$, which satisfies $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by orthonormality. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}P=\sum_{a=1}^n P_{aa}=\sum_{a=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (u_j)_a\overline{(u_j)_a}=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{a=1}^n|(u_j)_a|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r1=r$, since each $u_j$ is a unit vector. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, L1, algebra]

3.1 The operator in step 2.1 is independent of all allowed basis choices, lies in $\mathcal P_r$ by [L1], and is exactly the map specified by [F2]. Hence it is the unique rank-$r$ occupied spectral projector. [step 2.1, F2, L1] ∎

## Statement

Every $P\in\mathcal P_r$ belongs to the admissible density domain
$\mathcal D_r$.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $P\in\mathbb H_n$ satisfies $P=P^*$, $P^2=P$, and $\operatorname{tr}P=r$, where $1\le r<n$.

[F1] The rank-$r$ projector set is $\mathcal P_r=\{P=P^*:P^2=P,\operatorname{tr}P=r\}$ ([[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]).

[F2] A finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis and real eigenvalues ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F3] The admissible domain consists of Hermitian positive contractions of trace $r$ ([[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]]).

## Proof


1.1 By [F2], choose a unitary eigenbasis of $P$ with real eigenvalues $\mu_j$. From $P^2=P$, each satisfies $\mu_j^2=\mu_j$, hence $\mu_j\in\{0,1\}$. Therefore every eigenvalue lies between $0$ and $1$, so for each $x$ the quadratic forms $x^*Px$ and $x^*(I-P)x$ are nonnegative. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The matrix $P$ is Hermitian and has trace $r$ by [F1]; step 1.1 gives $0\preceq P\preceq I$. These are exactly the conditions in [F3], so $P\in\mathcal D_r$. [step 1.1, F1, F3] ∎

## Statement

For $n\ge2$ and $1\le r<n$, the set $\mathcal D_r$ of
[[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]] is nonempty, closed, and convex in
$\mathbb H_n$, and complete in the Frobenius metric.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Integers $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, the real vector space $\mathbb H_n$ with Frobenius norm, and $\mathcal D_r=\{D=D^*:0\preceq D\preceq I_n,\operatorname{tr}D=r\}$.

[F1] The domain and its order conditions are as in [[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]].

[F2] Every Euclidean Cauchy sequence in a finite-dimensional real coordinate space converges ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]).

## Proof


1.1 The diagonal matrix $D_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)$ with $r$ ones is Hermitian, satisfies $0\preceq D_0\preceq I_n$, and has trace $r$. Thus $D_0\in\mathcal D_r$, so the domain is nonempty. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Let $(D_k)$ be a Frobenius-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_r$. Each real and imaginary matrix entry is Cauchy because $| (D_k-D_\ell)_{ij}|\le\|D_k-D_\ell\|_F$. By [F2] the finitely many coordinates converge, defining a matrix $D$; conjugate symmetry passes to coordinate limits, so $D=D^*$. [given, F2]

2.1 For every fixed $x\in\mathbb C^n$, entrywise convergence gives $x^*D_kx\to x^*Dx$ and $x^*(I_n-D_k)x\to x^*(I_n-D)x$. Since both sequences are nonnegative, their limits are nonnegative, so $0\preceq D\preceq I_n$. Finite sums commute with coordinate limits, hence $\operatorname{tr}D=\lim_k\operatorname{tr}D_k=r$. Therefore $D\in\mathcal D_r$. [step 1.2, F1, algebra]

3.1 The finitely many entries converge, so the sum of their squared absolute errors tends to zero; thus $\|D_k-D\|_F\to0$. Every Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_r$ therefore converges there, proving completeness. Any ambient-convergent sequence in $\mathcal D_r$ is Cauchy, so the same limit argument shows its limit belongs to $\mathcal D_r$; this proves closedness. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1]

4.1 If $D_1,D_2\in\mathcal D_r$ and $t\in[0,1]$, then $tD_1+(1-t)D_2$ is Hermitian; its quadratic form and that of $I_n-tD_1-(1-t)D_2$ are convex combinations of nonnegative quadratic forms, and its trace is $t\operatorname{tr}D_1+(1-t)\operatorname{tr}D_2=tr+(1-t)r=r$. Hence it lies in $\mathcal D_r$, proving convexity. [F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$ have an occupied/unoccupied gap
$g=\lambda_{r+1}(H_0)-\lambda_r(H_0)>0$, and let $c,R,\Gamma$ be the circle
from [[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]. For Hermitian
$H$ in the open operator-norm ball $\|H-H_0\|_{op}<g/4$, let $\Pi_r(H)$ be its
projector onto the $r$ lowest eigenvalues. Then $H\mapsto\Pi_r(H)$ is real
Frechet $C^1$ in the Frobenius norm and
$$D\Pi_r(H)[E]=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma (zI-H)^{-1}E(zI-H)^{-1}\,dz$$
for each Hermitian direction $E$. With $\ell(\Gamma)=2\pi R$,
$$\|D\Pi_r(H)[E]\|_F\le\frac{16R}{g^2}\|E\|_F.$$
This is a block/cluster statement: no gap between eigenvalues inside either
cluster is required.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** $H_0\in\mathbb H_n$, $1\le r<n$, a gap $g>0$, and a Hermitian $H$ in the stated ball; write $R_H(z)=(zI-H)^{-1}$.

[F1] The fixed circle $\Gamma$ separates the first $r$ eigenvalues from the rest by distance at least $g/4$, and $\|R_H(z)\|_{op}\le4/g$ on $\Gamma$ ([[lem-spectral-gap-persistence-and-uniform-resolvent-bound]]).

[F2] A Hermitian matrix is unitarily diagonalizable with real eigenvalues ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]).

[F3] On a positively oriented circle, Cauchy's formula gives $\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma(z-\lambda)^{-1}dz=1$ for an interior $\lambda$; if $\lambda$ is outside, the integrand is holomorphic on the disk and its integral is zero ([[thm-cauchy-integral-formula-circle]], [[thm-cauchy-theorem-one-exceptional-point-on-a-star-shaped-domain]]).

[F4] The complex line integral is linear, exists for continuous functions on a rectifiable contour, and obeys the triangle inequality by its Riemann-sum definition ([[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]], [[prop-linearity-of-complex-line-integrals]], [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]).

[F5] The real Frechet derivative is the linear first-order approximation on real matrix spaces ([[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]]).

3.1 For any matrix $A$ and matrix $X$ with columns $x_j$, the operator-norm definition gives $\|AX\|_F^2=\sum_j\|Ax_j\|_2^2\le\|A\|_{op}^2\|X\|_F^2$.
